en: The *Wuliangshouguan jing yiji* (Record of the Meaning of the Sutra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus) states that one may attain the Way through empty words.

For this reason, although such a person does not undergo the suffering and affliction of birth and death, their bodhisattva faculties are dull and they cannot swiftly achieve Buddhahood; it is not direct.
"Going" is precisely the meaning of "bodhisattva. Question:
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born in the Pure Land, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* judge this to be of "intentional meaning regarding another time"? Answer:
This is stated as being "intended for another time" (paryāyābhiprāya) because it refers to those who do not practice;
thus the treatise says:
"By merely making a vow, one attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss."
This is called the "intention regarding another time.
According to this, a person who lacks practice merely makes vows in vain;
because these serve only as a remote cause for future birth, it is said to be an intention regarding another time.
One must practice both the vows and the conduct in order to attain rebirth there. Question:
Just as ordinary beings cannot be born in the higher realms without severing the afflictions of the desire realm, there are no ordinary beings who have severed the afflictions of all three realms.
By what means can one be born in the Pure Land? Answer:

Just as an ordinary person, though not having completely severed the seeds of afflictions in the desire realm, can be born in the form realm by suppressing those afflictions to be born in a higher realm.
This is likewise: by contemplating the Pure Land through the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), one deeply subdues and deeply reviles the afflictions of the triple world.
Because one subdues the coarse grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, one attains birth in the Pure Land. Question:
Question: Bodhisattvas resolve their minds to rescue suffering sentient beings;
why then do they vow to be born in a Pure Land? Answer:
Bodhisattvas vow to be born in a Pure Land in order to make offerings to all Buddhas.
I vow to enter the evil realms to rescue those suffering;
I vow to be born in the Pure Land to accomplish the Buddha-dharma;
I vow to enter the evil realms to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
These two practices must be constantly cultivated; one cannot be omitted.
Furthermore, whenever one wishes to rescue sentient beings from their suffering and affliction, one must first take birth in a Pure Land.
One naturally accomplishes the Buddha-dharma first,
and only thereafter enters the evil realms through the power of great compassionate vows to benefit sentient beings.
If one were to enter the evil realms before accomplishing the Buddha-dharma, [it would be impossible].
This means that one is bound by suffering oneself;
how, then, could one save sentient beings?
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
One must first benefit oneself,
and only then benefit others.
If one desires to benefit others before having benefited oneself, [it will not succeed].
It is like a person who, not having yet mastered the art of swimming, wishes to cross over;
they and their companion both sink together.
This case is also like that. Question:
If Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) are born in the Pure Land,
why does the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), in its explanation of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), state:
"One contemplates all phenomena as being without arising and without abiding"?
Even though they have entered the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and their minds are stilled, they continue to take birth within the three realms.
Why is this? Because the karmic tendencies and their resultant retributions have not yet been destroyed or exhausted.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"A bodhisattva of the lineage may fall into the evil realms.
Since it further says they "take birth within the three realms," [it follows that they do so].
Question: How can it be said that they are born in the Pure Land? Answer:
This refers to the fact that Bodhisattvas, out of great compassion for sentient beings, take birth within the three realms.
Because their karma is not yet exhausted and remains in correspondence with them, it is said that they take birth in the three realms or may fall into the evil destinies.

Now, regarding the statement "born in the Pure Land," this refers to being born in the Pure Land based on the maturation of one's own karmic retribution. From here on, the following explains the text according to the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, which clarifies only the three grades.
Within this, the practices for rebirth in the nine grades have been fully discussed in their various forms;
here, they differ only in being presented more extensively or concisely.
The nine grades in the text are thus divided into nine sections.
The middle section of the superior grade is divided into four parts:
first, the title of the chapter;
second, the manifestation of its characteristics.
Third, the signs of rebirth;
fourth, the summary.
The first section is easily understood.
Regarding the phrase "if there are sentient beings" within the section on the modes of practice (*ākāra*),
this refers to those at the stage of rebirth who are positioned at the final moment of mind of the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī pariṇāmanā*).
The reason for this is that once they have been born in that land, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, as for the arousal of these three types of mind:
within this stage, other practices have already been accomplished;
one arouses these three minds with the aspiration to attain rebirth there.
A sincere mind is one that is free from deceitful thoughts;
a profound mind is one that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones.
Regarding the mind of dedication and aspiration:
it is the vow to be reborn [in a pure land] by means of all the roots of goodness one has cultivated.
Furthermore, there are three kinds.
From here below, the specific characteristics are explained individually.
One who possesses all the practices of the precepts cultivates the samādhi of loving-kindness.
They uphold the threefold bodhisattva precepts.
Those who read and recite the Mahāyāna study the inconceivable and profound Dharma elucidated within the Vaipulya sūtras.
Those who read and recite it shall likewise attain inconceivable merit, and by virtue of this, they will be born in the Pure Land.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"If good men or good women hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and with a pure heart believe and revere it without giving rise to doubt or confusion..."
One will not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, but will be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
"lotus-birth by transformation" is precisely this meaning. This refers to those who practice the six recollections.
That which is called mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, giving, precepts, and devas:
mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha serves to generate merit;
mindfulness of giving and the precepts serves as spiritual practice.
Those who practice mindfulness of the devas do so with the thought that they will be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven as a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood;
they dedicate these three kinds of roots of goodness toward the aspiration for such a rebirth.
"From one day to seven days" refers to this period.
Regarding the period for practicing the clear conduct:
if one maintains the continuity of mind-moment after mind-moment with the aforementioned preparatory practices throughout seven days, one will attain rebirth.
The reason for this is as follows:
Because the power of karma is inconceivable, even as a single thought arises—
if one slanders the Mahāyāna— one shall undergo the retribution of suffering in the great hells of the ten directions for kalpa after kalpa.
Although the duration was brief, the retribution for suffering was extreme;
yet, in this same way, because the power of their wholesome karma was great despite the brevity of the time spent, they were able to be born in that land.
How true it is!
The power of karma is inconceivable; in the space of a single moment, beings may rise or sink in different ways.
Therefore, this practitioner must strictly admonish themselves.
Is this not indeed a matter of great importance? Next, the signs of rebirth will be explained.
First, the palace welcomes [the Bodhisattva];
second, light illuminates his body;
third, his deeds and practices are praised.
The fourth clearly explains rebirth;
the fifth explains awakening to the Way after being born there.
As for those who are reborn in that land in the time it takes to snap one's fingers:
Due to the predominance of karmic power, rebirth occurs with great swiftness;
this differs from the human realm, where rebirth is only attained after a long time because karmic power is weak and inferior.
Just as one enters the evil destinies in an instant due to the intensity of evil karma.
"This is likewise so: 'one who immediately awakens to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas' refers to the patience of non-arising in the first stage (bhūmi).
'Serving various Buddhas through successive stages'..."
Because they have attained supreme supernormal powers (abhijñā), they are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the Buddhas.
Just as the gods, upon being born, are immediately able to fly through the void,
so too is this the case here.
Successive prediction (*anupūrva-vyākaraṇa*) is also called "bestowal of prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*).
"Bestowal" (*vyā*) means to grant.
That person receives it; that very person accepts it.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, for six reasons, the Tathāgata bestows the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of unsurpassed bodhi upon them.
First, those of a single lineage who have not yet resolved their minds;
second, those of a single lineage who have already resolved their minds;
third, those who are present before one.
Fourth, non-manifestation;
fifth, fixed duration;
sixth, indefinite duration.
What is clarified here is the "present-life prediction" (*pratyutpanna-vyākaraṇa*). From this point downward, the summary can be understood.
Next, the birth of those of superior capacity and middling birth is explained;
there are four sections within this text.
First, the title of the chapter is indicated;
second, the characteristics of practice are clarified;
third, the signs of rebirth are explained.
Fourth, the summary:

This refers to Bodhisattvas at the stages of the Ten Understandings and above, who, by being born in that land, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within a single minor kalpa.

The phrase "not necessarily upholding the scriptures" distinguishes these from those mentioned previously; such persons engage solely in the practice of the Mahāyāna rather than the activity of reading and reciting.
"One who well understands the meaning and intent" is one who is skillfully able to discern the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna without destroying conventional designations,
while yet explaining the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. "One whose mind is not startled or shaken regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)" means:
The profound meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna is the most supreme among all dharmas;
therefore, it is called "foremost.
When ordinary beings hear it said that all dharmas are empty, their reasoning contradicts their worldly sentiments, and thus they give rise to alarm and fear.
When a bodhisattva hears this, they profoundly penetrate the source of the mind and give rise to no fear.
Those who have deep faith in cause and effect achieve right view as soon as a single thought arises;
those with wrong views slander [the truth] by denying cause and effect.
Thus, having severed their roots of goodness, they sought to sink into the sea of suffering;
now, by virtue of profound faith, they have attained birth in the Pure Land. Regarding those who do not slander the Mahāyāna:
the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma are exceedingly profound.
Its phrasing is skillful and subtle;
the noble ones of the three vehicles all cultivate and study it together,
thereby giving rise to all the fruits and retributions of humans and devas.
It gives birth to the noble paths of the three vehicles.
If one slanders this Dharma, the resulting offense is immeasurable;
yet if one hears it and does not slander it, the merit thereof is likewise impossible to fully describe.
Therefore, the *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Suppose Jambudvīpa, measuring seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth,

were completely filled with stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as densely packed as bamboo or hemp stalks, such that there were not even the slightest void or gap between them."
If there were a son or daughter of good family who provided the four requisites of support for the entire lifespan of a noble one,
or who filled this continent with the seven treasures, piling them up as high as the Brahma-heaven;
When each and every noble person has completed giving that many [gifts],
this son or daughter of good family shall have a lifespan of thirty *muyuda* days and nights, continuing without interruption.
If a son or daughter of good family does not slander this sūtra,
their merit will surpass that [of the former], such that even a hundredth part,
a thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-millionth part cannot equal it.
It is even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Because their merit is boundless, they are able to be born in the Pure Land. From here on, the characteristics of birth [in the Pure Land] will be explained.
First, the World-Honored One’s reception is clarified;
second, his merits are praised;
third, rebirth therein is correctly explained.
Regarding the statement that those of the Fourth Clarification awaken to the Way upon birth and attain non-retrogression in Bodhi after seven days:
from the stage of the Ten Understandings (daśa-vijñāna) upward, there still remains the possibility of retrogression through thought or retrogression through practice.
Having reached that land, one is free from these two types of regression;
because there are no conditions for regression,
one never regresses from the fruit attained, just as in the heavens.
Because there are no conditions for regression, this is also like that.
One who attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) after one intermediate kalpa realizes the patience of non-arising of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
If one were to calculate the kalpas according to this present world-system, it would pass through immeasurable great kalpas;
however, since we are now speaking of the kalpa count of that land, it is referred to as a single "small kalpa" (antarakalpa).
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"One kalpa in the Sahā world constitutes a single day and night in the Abhirati world;
this is what is meant. From here below, the summary can be understood.
From here below, the next section clarifies those who are born in the lower grade of the superior class.
The text contains four sections:
first, the title of the chapter;
second, the manifestation of its characteristics.
Third, the signs of rebirth in the three [pure] realms;
fourth, the general conclusion.
The initial text is easily understood.
Regarding "also cause and effect":
this refers to the accomplishment of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) within the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*); because of this, one does not slander the Mahāyāna.
By virtue of believing in the Mahāyāna, one generates the mind set on the unsurpassed path (*anuttara-mārga-citta*).
By means of these merits, one dedicates them with the vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. From here on, the signs of rebirth are clarified:
first, the welcoming by transformation Buddhas;
second, the praise of their merit.
Third, it clearly explains rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Fourth, it explains the realization of the Way.
As for those who attain the vision of the Buddha within seven days:
Because he had not yet attained the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it was only after seven days that he beheld the Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "after passing through three minor kalpas, he attained the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwelt in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)," if one calculates by the kalpa-numbers of this world-system,
it would be only after three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* that one reaches the first stage.
Now, by means of the kalpa-measure of that land as well, one passes through three minor kalpas to reach the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As for the "Clarifying Gateway of the Hundred Dharmas" (*Śatadharma-vyākhyāna-mukha*),
it is as explained in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Jewel Garland).
The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) possess ten mental factors (*caitta*), namely:

the mind of faith, the mind of diligence, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of concentration, the mind of wisdom, the mind of non-retrogression, the mind of dedication, the mind of protecting the Dharma, the mind of aspiration, and the mind of precepts.
Within each of these ten minds, there are further ten minds; thus, there are one hundred. From here on, the concluding summary is easily understood.
The above has clarified the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (Tri-śaikṣa) in the Mahāyāna.
These are for the three types of persons of superior grade.
From this point downward, the stages of skillful means of the Hīnayāna are clarified;
these are for the three types of persons of middling grade.
First, the superior birth of the middle grade is explained.
Within this section, there are four parts:
first, the title of the chapter is presented.
First, the manifestation of the mode of practice;
second, the manifestation of the signs of rebirth; third, the explanation of the signs of rebirth;
fourth, the summary conclusion.
The initial passage is easily understood.

As for the statement, "If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold the five precepts," this clarifies that the stage of such rebirthers is at the levels of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summits).
Within this stage, one generates the bodhicitta and dedicates it with the vow to be reborn in a pure land.
This applies to both laypeople and monastics;
however, since this passage clarifies the case of laypeople, it mentions "observing the five precepts and the eight precepts."
Regarding "those who practice the various precepts," this clarifies that it refers to those who have left the household life;
because they fully receive the great bhikṣu vows, they are said to "practice the various precepts."
Those who do not commit the five heinous crimes—
this karma is extremely grave;
having committed such karma, one will inevitably enter hell in the very next life.
Therefore, one cannot be born in the Pure Land.
According to the Śrāvaka vehicle, while at the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat), one may still commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and sever the roots of goodness;
at the stage of *mūrdhan* (Summit), one may commit the five heinous crimes but does not sever the roots of goodness.
Therefore, this karma is now eliminated.
As for those who dedicate their merit with the vow to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss,
these individuals have practiced until they reach the stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit).
Because the faculties and dispositions of those in the Hīnayāna are not yet determined,
they may suddenly encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and give rise to the Mahāyāna bodhicitta;
they then dedicate the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward the aspiration to be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

If one reaches the stage of *kṣānti* (receptivity), the root-nature of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is already fixed, and since rebirth in the evil destinies has been extinguished, it is no longer possible to turn toward seeking the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). From here on, the characteristics of rebirth [in the Pure Land] will be explained.
First, the World-Honored One’s reception;
second, the praise of renunciation;
third, the clarification of rebirth in the right place.
The fourth clarifies that after birth, one awakens to the Way;
those who praise the Four Noble Truths are those who hear the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
Because the practitioner previously practiced the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), due to the power of that repeated practice, they again hear the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths:
the first is the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
The first has the five aggregates as its essence.
The second is the truth of origination,
which has karma and afflictions as its essence.
The third is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*),
which has analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence.
The fourth is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
One who has attained arhatship takes uncontaminated noble wisdom as their essence.
Because this person possesses sharp faculties and has undergone three births, they immediately attain the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
As for "arhat":
This is called "unborn" (anutpāda) and is also named "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
As for the "three knowledges" (trividyā):
1. The clear knowledge of past lives;
2. The clear knowledge of the divine eye;
3. The clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
In the Hīnayāna school, the first two [knowledges] have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as their essence,
while the third has untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) as its essence.
According to the Mahāyāna, the first two have subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence.
The third [body] has non-conceptual wisdom as its essence. Regarding the six supernormal powers (abhijñā):
first, the power of psychic transformation (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna);
second, the power of the divine eye (divya-cakṣus).
Third, the supernormal power of the divine ear;
fourth, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others;
fifth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

According to the Hīnayāna school, the supernormal powers of psychic mobility (*ṛddhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), and the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as their nature.
The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) has five knowledges as its nature.

This refers to the nine types of knowledge consisting of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), excluding conventional knowledge because its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*). According to the Mahāyāna school, the first five supernormal powers have subsequent knowledge as their essential nature.
The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) has non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as its essence. Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*):
first, possessing internal form, one perceives external forms;
second, being without internal form, one perceives external forms.
3. The liberation of the pure [perception];
4. the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 5.
the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness;
seventh, the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
eighth, the liberation of cessation.
In the Hīnayāna school, the first three liberations have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their essence;
the next four liberations have the four [immeasurables] as their essence;
and the liberation of cessation has that which is neither form nor conditioned as its essence.

Based on the Mahāyāna, those attained from the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vijñapti*) upward, the first seven [liberations] all take uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as their essence.
The liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*) first takes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as its essence at the level of the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Because all mind and mental factors do not function, the following summary can be understood.
Next, the middle grade within the intermediate [rebirth] is explained;
there are four sections in this passage.
First, the title of the chapter is indicated;
second, the characteristics of practice are revealed;
third, the signs of rebirth are clarified.
Fourth, the summary:
"If there are sentient beings" clarifies that the practitioner's stage resides within the general and specific foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Those who observe the eight precepts are householders;
those who possess the śrāmaṇera precepts and the full precepts are renunciants.
"One whose deportment is without deficiency" means one who does not violate even the minor precepts.
When a practitioner reaches this stage, they may suddenly encounter a virtuous friend of the Mahāyāna, who inspires them to generate the Mahāyāna bodhicitta.
This is the dedication of merit with the vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
From here on, the characteristics of rebirth are clarified.
First, the World-Honored One’s reception [of the practitioner] is explained.
Second, praising through transformed sounds;
third, clearly explaining rebirth;
fourth, clarifying the realization of the Way after being born there.
Regarding those who attain the stage of *srotāpanna* after seven days:
because they previously practiced the contemplative methods of the Hīnayāna, they attain the first fruit;
it is only after another half-aeon that they become *aśaikṣas*. Question:
That land is said to be this world-system for seven kalpas.
This person has already cultivated the roots of merit conducive to liberation;
why then does it take seven kalpas before they attain the first fruit? Answer:
The faculties and dispositions of śrāvakas are of three types:
first, those who attain [enlightenment] in three lifetimes;
second, those who attain it in sixty kalpas.
"Three hundred kalpas.
This refers to those of middling faculties; therefore, they attain [the fruit] only after seven kalpas. From here below, the summary can be understood.
From here below, the next section clarifies those of the middle grade who are born in the lower realm.
The text contains four parts:
first, the title of the chapter;
second, the manifestation of its characteristics.
Third, the signs of rebirth;
fourth, the summary.
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family... [and so forth].
This clarifies that the stage of rebirth for such a person lies within the stage of the five preparatory concentrations (*pañca-vinirukti-citta*).
Regarding those who filially support their parents:
this refers to the field of gratitude (*upakāra-kṣetra*), wherein making offerings to it yields great karmic fruit.
Regarding those who have practiced human virtues— such as righteousness, propriety, and yielding— when such persons approach their end of life,

they may suddenly encounter a virtuous friend of the Mahāyāna who explains for them the joyful matters of the Pure Land and praises the Great Vows made by the World-Honored One during his causal practices.
Having heard this, such a person dedicates their merit with the vow to be reborn there.
Following this, the characteristics of rebirth will be clarified;
first, rebirth itself is explained.
Next, the realization of the Way after birth is explained.
Because this person’s roots of goodness were inferior, they lacked the karmic power to induce the World-Honored One to come and welcome them;
thus, they attained birth spontaneously.
Regarding the statement that one becomes an Arhat only after the passage of a small kalpa:
because this person first cultivates the practice of contemplation (vipaśyanā), it is only upon reaching the end of that kalpa that they attain the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa). Question:
Having been born in the Pure Land, one cultivates the path of a bodhisattva together with others.
How is it that one can still attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle? Answer:
The categories of the Buddhas’ Pure Lands are manifold and vast.
There are pure lands where even the names of the two vehicles do not exist,
such as the World of Universal Fragrance, the World of Unblinking Eyes,
and others. There are also pure lands.
There are names for the two vehicles as well as for humans and devas,
just as in the world of Abhirati;
or there may be pure lands [without such designations].
There are no followers of the two vehicles, nor humans or devas,
as in the world of Ultimate Bliss;
these people have all previously cultivated the roots of goodness of the Small Vehicle in this land.
Therefore, having been born in that land, they rely on what they previously practiced to attain the fruits of the Hīnayāna;
yet, although they have attained these small fruits, they do not realize them as final,
but instead cultivate the path of a Bodhisattva, which is distinct [from the Hīnayāna].
Because one attains the fruit in this very life and abides therein without further progress,
preserving its original name, it is called "Arhat.
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans, and devas therein possess lofty wisdom and penetrating supernatural powers;
they are all of one kind, their forms being without distinction,
yet they bear the names "human" or "deva" merely because they conform to other regions.
This is precisely its meaning. The summary from below can be understood accordingly.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the three types of persons of middle capacity.
From here on, the three types of persons of lower capacity will be explained.
These are all individuals among ordinary beings who have resolved to attain bodhicitta.
First, the superior birth of the lower grade is explained;
there are four sections within this passage.
First, the title of the chapter is indicated;
second, the characteristics of practice are revealed;
third, rebirth is clarified.
Fourth, the summary:
"There may be sentient beings who commit various evil deeds.
This clarifies the aspect of their conduct.
This person, having previously resolved upon bodhicitta, suddenly encounters adverse conditions and commits the ten unwholesome karmas.
Because these evil dharmas increase, their mind becomes devoid of shame and remorse. Thus far, the faults have been elucidated.
Next, I shall clarify his virtues.

That is to say, when his life was about to end, because a virtuous friend praised the names of Mahāyāna sūtras for him and recited the name of the World-Honored One Amitābha, he was able to eliminate his grave sins.
The reason for this is that because the Tathāgata’s field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is pure,
one obtains inconceivable blessings by merely reciting his name; thus, one is able to extinguish even grave offenses.

Just as giving rise to a single thought of malice and slandering a sage leads to suffering for many kalpas, now, by virtue of a single thought of faith and invoking the Name, one experiences joy for many kalpas.
That cause and effect are thus necessarily distinct cannot be considered an error. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
The Buddha told the devaputras:
"If there are devaputras or devakanyās whose lives are about to end,
you should simply recite the Prajñāpāramitā for them."
Because they have heard the name of the Prajñāpāramitā, the sons of the gods are not born into the evil realms, but are reborn among the devas. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"If there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Buddha..."
I declare that such a person will certainly attain entry into nirvāṇa.
If there are sentient beings who, out of mindfulness of the Buddha, scatter even a single flower into the air,
the karmic fruit and reward obtained from such merit will be inexhaustible.
If there are sentient beings who, with a heart of utmost sincerity, recollect the merit of the Buddha and scatter even a single flower into the air,
they shall in future ages attain the status of Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devānām-indra, or a Cakravartin Universal Monarch.
Even their karmic rewards cannot be exhausted.
Because the karmic rewards of their roots of goodness are inexhaustible, they must eventually enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Ānanda, the field of merit that one offers to the Buddha cannot be exhausted by the fruits of conditioned existence.
I declare that such a person will certainly attain nirvāṇa and reach the very limit of nirvāṇa.
Ānanda, even for those who recite the name of the Buddha but once and give rise to faith for a single lifetime,
the merit they have created shall never be in vain.
Should there be sentient beings with pure hearts who likewise utter this name, saying "Namo Buddha," [the same applies].
Ānanda, by means of these roots of goodness, that person will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
To "attain proximity to nirvāṇa," "flow toward it in continuous succession," and "enter the limit of nirvāṇa" is precisely what this means.
From here on, the next section clarifies the signs of rebirth.
First, it clarifies the welcoming by the transformation buddhas;
second, it praises their merits;
third, it correctly elucidates rebirth there.
Regarding the statement that Simhamati had already awakened to the Way and entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) after ten minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*):
because he was still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it was necessary for him to be born there and undergo ten minor kalpas before he could finally enter the first stage.
Regarding those who attain rebirth simply by hearing the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha:
furthermore, there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death, hear the names of the Triple Gem and immediately attain rebirth.
The reason for this is as follows:
Because the merit of the jewels is inconceivable,
it enables those who hear [this teaching] to be born in the Pure Land.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
By means of their supernormal powers, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas fly to all places throughout the ten directions where the names of the Three Jewels are not found.
To praise the merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
they cause sentient beings who hear them to be reborn before the presence of the Buddhas.
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
"If there are sentient beings who, for even a single thought-moment, have deep faith in the Tathāgata,
regarding him with reverence and respect, and exclaiming that he is unprecedented."
By virtue of reverence and faith, one attains the status of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who governs the four continents and possesses the seven treasures;
furthermore, one may even become Śakra Devendra, Māra, or Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World.
How much more so for those who are constantly able to possess faith in the Triple Gem;
this is the meaning.
From here on, the next section clarifies rebirth in the middle grade of the lower level.
The text consists of four parts:
first, the title of the chapter;
second, the manifestation of its characteristics.
Third, the signs of rebirth in the three realms;
fourth, the summary.
There may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts.
This clarifies the person who attains rebirth there.
First, their transgressions are revealed:
those who violate the five precepts or the eight precepts are householders.
One who has received full ordination is a renunciant.
"To steal the property of the Saṃgha" refers to the property belonging to the permanently resident Saṃgha of the ten directions.
"Property belonging to the present Saṃgha" refers to the goods belonging to the persons currently residing at a single monastic dwelling.
"Impure preaching of the Dharma" refers to...
To preach the reality-mark (dharmatā) of all phenomena while motivated by personal gain and fame, or to do so for the sake of defeating others, is called impure preaching of the Dharma.
As for "the fierce fires of hell arriving all at once": it refers to this.
Once the evil causes have been established, the evil signs of the intermediate state (antarābhava) manifest.
To encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) who explains the ten powers of Amitābha Buddha clarifies his virtues.
They are called "powers" (*bala*) because they can destroy false pride;
they all have wisdom as their essence.
One wisdom resides in ten locations.
Regarding those named the "Ten Powers":
first is the power of the possible and the impossible;
second is the power of karma.
Third, the power of concentration;
fourth, the power of the faculties;
fifth, the power of desire.
Sixth, the power of the natures;
seventh, the power of the path to all destinations;
eighth, the power of recollecting past lives.
Ninth is the power of the divine eye;
tenth is the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Regarding "majestic power" (vaśitā): the supernormal powers that cause the cessation of pride are called majestic power.
He also praised those who possess morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
these constitute the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body.
The body of morality has the three clusters of pure precepts as its essence.
The body of wisdom has all-knowledge as its essence;
the body of concentration has all meditative absorptions, such as the Mahāyāna-prakāśa samādhi, as its essence;
and the body of liberation has both conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation as its essence.
The body of knowledge and vision of liberation has post-attainment wisdom as its essence.
From here below, the benefits are explained:
namely, that by hearing of the Tathāgata’s merits, one eliminates the transgressions of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
The reason for this is that the name and the merits of the Tathāgata are both impossible to hear; yet,
if one hears his name, the merit obtained shall be immeasurable.
The *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"That which is called the recollection of the Buddha's merits refers to his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."
A golden-colored body with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,
and the eighteen unique qualities.
Regarding the three foundations of mindfulness of great compassion:
if there are sentient beings who hear but once of the Buddha’s body and its aforementioned marks, signs, and radiance,
they shall not fall into the evil realms nor give rise to false views for billions upon billions of kalpas.
Even in places of various evils, one will always attain right view and practice with diligent perseverance without ceasing.
Merely hearing the name of the Buddha brings forth such merit as this.
How much more so for the samādhi of focused mindfulness on the Buddha—this is precisely its meaning.
From here on, the characteristics of rebirth are explained;
first, the cessation of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is clarified.
First, the fierce fires of hell are transformed into a cool breeze;
second, transformation Buddhas come to welcome one;
third, one attains rebirth in the pure land.
The four types of birth have already received benefit.
Because this person’s karmic power is inferior, the lotus flower will only open after six kalpas. From here below, the summary can be understood.
From here below, the characteristics of the lower grade of the lower birth are explained.
The text contains four parts:
first, the designation of the chapter title;
second, the manifestation of the modes of practice.
Third, the signs of rebirth;
fourth, the summary.
There may be sentient beings who perform unwholesome deeds.
This clarifies the characteristics [of the offense].
First, its faults are clarified.
Regarding the five heinous crimes (ānantarya):
Killing one's father;
harming one's mother;
killing an arhat.
Drawing blood from the Buddha’s body and causing a schism in the harmonious Sangha. Question:
The *Anantarya-sūtra* states:
"Excepting only those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma."
Question: Why is it that those who have committed the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya) can be born in the Pure Land? Answer:
There are two types of persons who commit the five heinous crimes.
The first refers to a person who initially resolves to attain bodhicitta,
but in the interim suddenly commits the five heinous crimes.
Later, by virtue of correctly reciting the Buddha’s name, they suppress and extinguish their karmic obstructions and attain birth in the Pure Land.
This sutra discusses these two cases based on the following:
this person previously lacked the bodhicitta and further committed the five heinous crimes,
and moreover, possessed no merit from recollecting the Buddha.
This person is not reborn [in the evil realms].
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* speaks on the basis of this.
Below, its virtues are elucidated.
"A virtuous friend who expounds the sublime Dharma" refers to one who teaches the Mahāyāna.
"Hearing the Mahāyāna sūtras can eliminate grave offenses and instructing one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha" means this.
The merit of mindfulness of the Buddha can eliminate karmic obstructions.
To say one "has no leisure for mindfulness of the Buddha" means that one lacks the opportunity.
This person, being oppressed by the suffering of death, has no leisure to contemplate the Buddha’s merits or his name.
"Possessing ten recitations" clarifies the duration of time;
the karma of these ten recitations can eliminate grave offenses and lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There are those who have committed evil throughout their lives yet are born into a good realm at the time of death;
there are those who have performed good throughout their lives yet are born into an evil realm at the time of death."
This has two meanings:
first, because karma to be experienced in a subsequent life has matured;
second, because wholesome states of mind and mental factors arise at the time of death. Question:
Question: This person has committed evil throughout their entire life.
How can a single thought at the moment of death overcome the karmic actions performed during their whole lifetime? Answer:
It is like a great general who, as a single individual, is able to defeat a massive enemy force.
The mind at the moment of death is likewise.
Like fire or like poison, a single thought-moment can overcome the deeds of an entire lifetime;
it can overcome the karmic actions performed throughout one's whole life.
This is precisely the meaning of "because one abandons the urgent affairs of the sense faculties. From here on, the signs of rebirth are clarified;
first, one sees a lotus flower.
Second, the explicit explanation of rebirth;
third, the clarification of the benefits already obtained.
To explain these extensively is to teach the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This refers to the ultimate depth of the Mahāyāna.
For it is said that if one contemplates [this], even grave offenses can be extinguished.
As the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who contemplate the ultimate truth of the profoundly deep dharma of emptiness,
they eliminate the sins of a million billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of birth and death in the space of a single finger-snap.
Such a person is called one who is fully endowed with the bodhisattva precepts.
It is not necessary to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), for it is naturally accomplished;
that this one should receive the offerings of all humans and devas is precisely its meaning.
From here on, the concluding summary is clear and requires no further explanation.
The preceding section has concluded the answers to the questions, demonstrating the characteristics of contemplation.
From here on, the second part clarifies the benefits obtained by the assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage of Dedication (daśamī-pratipannaka), having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the characteristics of the Pure Land, [attained realization].
He immediately attained the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha,
beheld the marks of the adornments of the World of Ultimate Bliss,
and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Question:

Since they are bodhisattvas of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), why does the preceding text say, "You are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) whose mental conceptions are weak and inferior"? Answer:
From the perspective of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), all bodhisattvas prior to that stage are designated as ordinary beings.
This is because they have not yet realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). From this point downward, the aspiration is clarified:
having heard the rare Dharma and further realized the Dharma-body, they therefore make a vow to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Just as the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna,
having realized the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) here, made a vow to be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*),
so it is in this case as well.
This sutra specifically teaches that those of the highest grade of the highest birth are precisely [those described here].
If one were to say that Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage constitute those of the highest grade of the highest birth,
how could it be that the retribution of a sixth-stage Bodhisattva lies in a defiled land, yet they make a vow to be born in a pure land?
Because Bodhisattvas prior to the stages have not yet exhausted their karmic bonds and afflictions, they are born in defiled lands.
For this reason, they make vows here to be reborn in a Pure Land.
Thus, the meaning of the text is self-evident and requires no further elaboration.
Having been born in that land and attained the samādhi of the presence of all Buddhas,
one acquires all the faculties upon birth and constantly beholds all Buddhas without the need for further cultivation.
Because it is seen for the first time, it is called the Samādhi of Presence (Pratyutpanna-samādhi).

Since the celestial maidens and goddesses saw that the lady had attained realization, they looked up to this superior stream [of practice] and all gave rise to the bodhicitta. From here below begins the third section, clarifying the *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) portion.
The text consists of five parts:
first, the Venerable Ānanda requests instruction on upholding the Dharma;
second, the Tathāgata establishes the title of the sūtra.
1. Triple praise for the benefits of cultivation;
2. The assembly rejoices at four times;
3. The Tathāgata returns.
The first two passages are intelligible.
Regarding the statement within the praise of the benefits of cultivation that one "manifests a body and sees the Buddha," this clarifies the benefit in the present life.
By the power of samādhi, one who manifests the body will necessarily see the Buddha.
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The buddhānusmṛti-samādhi necessarily leads to seeing the Buddha."
This refers to the saying: "Upon the end of life, one will be reborn before the Buddha.
Next, the inferior is cited to manifest the superior.
If merely hearing the name of the Buddha and the names of these two bodhisattvas eliminates immeasurable sins,
how much more so for those who focus their minds and keep them in mind!
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
If one can bring the Tathāgata to mind for even a brief moment,
by the power of even a single thought of merit,
one will forever be freed from the three evil realms.
The light of wisdom extinguishes the darkness of delusion.
It is further said:
"It would be better to undergo all manner of suffering throughout immeasurable kalpas."

To hear the name of the Buddha means that one will not have to undergo all manner of sufferings throughout immeasurable kalpas; whereas to not hear the name of the Buddha is why one wanders through the suffering of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas—this is precisely its meaning.
The next section uses analogies to illustrate the Dharma.
As for the *pundarīka* flower,
it is the white lotus.
Just as this flower is the most excellent in the world,
so too is the practitioner who recollects the Buddha the most excellent among human beings.
Furthermore, because they constantly keep the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind, these two Bodhisattvas serve as their superior friends.
The following clarifies the benefits for the future:
by virtue of recollecting the merits of the Buddha, they will certainly attain Bodhi and sit at the site of enlightenment in the future.
Regarding the family of the Buddhas, there are two kinds of Buddha-families.
The first is the family of birth,
which refers to the retribution of the ten kings.
The second is the Dharma family,
which refers to the *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Because the practitioner recollects the Buddha, by virtue of that recollection, they will necessarily be born into the Buddha family.
Just as when a person thinks of being born in the heavens, they will surely attain it according to their wish, so it is with this.
As for the World-Honored One’s walking through the air back to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain:
previously, in order to enter the royal palace, he had secretly manifested supernatural powers to attend the invitation.
Now, when the Tathāgata manifests his majestic deportment so that those who see him may obtain merit,
his feet are always four inches above the ground as he walks, and the mark of the wheel (cakrāṅka) appears. Thus,
the *Huashou jing* (Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra) says:
When the Buddha walks, if there are sentient beings who touch his feet, they shall experience joy for seven days.
When the Tathāgata turns his body to the right, the earth sinks down eighty-four thousand yojanas, revolving like a wheel.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"When the Tathāgata enters or leaves cities, towns, villages, or houses, his feet do not tread upon the ground;
he always walks upon thousand-petaled lotuses."

If there are sentient beings who encounter the shadow of the Buddha, they shall enjoy peace and happiness for seven days without any desire for food or drink; after casting off this body, they will be reborn in a favorable existence.
This is called the benefit manifested through the Tathāgata’s active conduct.
The following clarifies the benefits of widespread propagation.
Since the Tathāgata preached the Dharma while in the royal palace,
he did not reach other people.
The Venerable Ānanda further proclaimed it extensively for the assembly;
upon hearing it, the great multitude were all filled with joy.
